This paper develops an RL-based controller enhanced by physics-informed policy, leveraging the advantages of both linear control models (data-efficient and interpretable) and RL models (flexible to multiple objectives and fast computing). We propose the Physics-Enhanced Residual Policy Learning (PERPL) framework, where the physics component provides model interpretability and stability. The learning-based Residual Policy adjusts the physics-based policy to adapt to the changing environment, thereby refining the decisions of the physics model. Theoretical analysis shows that, under local approximation conditions, PERPL can exhibit a smaller Lipschitz constant and less restrictive stability requirements compared to a pure RL policy. We apply the proposed model to decentralized cruising control in mixed traffic platoon of Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) and Human-driven Vehicles (HVs) with actuator and communication delays. Experimental results demonstrate that PERPL achieves smaller headway errors and better oscillation dampening than linear models and RL in unseen scenarios with artificially extreme conditions. title: GPU-accelerated heuristic parallel differential evolution for reaction wheel actuator fault identification in spacecraft attitude control systems
abstract: Reaction wheels, as core actuators in spacecraft attitude control systems, are prone to two prevalent faults: effectiveness degradation and additive torque biases. The reaction wheel dynamic model is integrated into the fault estimation framework to constrain the solution space and tackle the issue of multiple feasible solutions in redundant actuator fault identification. Meanwhile, the PDE algorithm encodes fault parameters as candidate solutions, leveraging evolutionary operations to converge to true fault values swiftly. Additionally, GPU parallelisation is employed to accelerate computationally intensive operations, markedly reducing inference time for onboard deployment. The proposed PDE method is further integrated with a reinforcement learning (RL)-based fault-tolerant controller, forming a closed-loop active fault-tolerant system. Experimental results demonstrate that the PDE method achieves an order-of-magnitude improvement in estimation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art FDI methods. The GPU-acceleration also yields significant speedups for the complicated search process, enabling real-time performance. This can be achieved either by placing the valve close to the actuator or by compensating for long pneumatic tubes through dynamic modeling. Tube compensation, however, is complex and difficult to implement, while direct valve mounting is often impractical because conventional proportional valves are large and heavy.To overcome these limitations, a compact, custom-designed 3/3-valve unit (CVU) based on Festo’s VEAE piezoelectric valves is developed. The CVU supports pressures up to 6bar, flow rates up to 70l/min and control bandwidths exceeding 9Hz. It is controlled using the presented data-driven approach, which eliminates the need for classical system identification and automatically adapts to different actuator volumes, resulting in high accuracy and simple deployment.The control scheme employs a two-stage, data-driven architecture based on single-shot Gaussian process (GP) regression. First, the inverse static flow characteristics of each valve are modeled, compensating for valve-to-valve variability without manual mass-flow identification. Second, the CVU is adapted to the actuator’s state-dependent volume, improving accuracy and robustness to external disturbances. In both stages, only the pressure derivative is used, avoiding the need for additional flow sensors or external test benches and keeping the approach lightweight and low-cost. The CVU with the data-driven control method was validated on an antagonistic pneumatic arm with pneumatic artificial muscles (PAMs) and benchmarked against a manually tuned PID controller, a feedback-linearized controller based on analytical system inversion and a commercially available VEAB valve unit. Across all tests, the CVU with GP-based control achieved highly accurate pressure tracking and disturbance rejection. All hardware (CAD) and development code (m-code) are released as open source.

title: Deep reinforcement learning in applied control: Challenges, analysis, and insights
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithms have shown increasing promise for autonomous decision-making and continuous control, yet their practical value relative to established control methods remains difficult to assess under realistic control-engineering conditions. Existing evaluations are often narrow, application-specific, or based on inconsistent assumptions. As a result, it remains unclear when learned controllers are suitable alternatives to conventional designs. This paper presents a systematic assessment framework that compares four prominent DRL controllers with a classical control baseline across a diverse set of applied control problems, including non-minimum phase dynamics, flexible mechanical systems, nonlinear marine control, and aerial robotics. The framework standardises modelling assumptions, reward design, controller tuning, computational budgets, performance metrics, robustness tests, and deployment conditions. This allows fair and reproducible analysis across methods and applications. The evaluation covers tracking accuracy, settling time, overshoot, control effort, actuator saturation, disturbance rejection, model uncertainty, robustness margins, and sim-to-real transfer. The results show that performance depends strongly on the algorithmic structure, system dynamics, and operating conditions. Learned controllers provide advantages in some cases, particularly for nonlinearities, constraints, and uncertain operating regimes. Classical control remains competitive in accuracy, simplicity, and reliability for several benchmark conditions. Under combined saturation and unmodelled dynamics, the learned controllers maintained stable operation where the classical baseline became unstable. Real-time deployment on a quadrotor platform further demonstrated stable sim-to-real transfer. The study establishes a rigorous and reproducible evidence base for assessing the practical suitability of these data-driven control algorithms in applied control. It clarifies the trade-offs between learning-based and conventional control. This addresses a critical gap that cannot be easily inferred from isolated, system-specific studies.

title: Support-boundary and relative-reliability diagnostics for hybrid memory–neural reinforcement learning
abstract: Hybrid reinforcement-learning controllers must distinguish supported memory use from unsupported neural extrapolation. The study develops an auditable support-boundary diagnostic protocol and evaluates relative-reliability arbitration. In a 30-seed application-shift test, k-nearest-neighbor and Gaussian-affinity support improve return AUC over exact count gating by 0.422 and 0.766, but remain below tabular Q-learning. The co-primary same-input crisp-versus-fuzzy contrast is generator-specific and favors crisp in the localized generator. Sensorized Crazyflie/PyBullet software-in-the-loop testing exposes a failure boundary: exact support collapses, tolerant kNN yields partial coverage without waypoint success, and learned controllers remain at zero success. A separately locked supplemental, non-confirmatory benchmark evaluates SAC, CrossQ, and TQC on HalfCheetah-v5 and Walker2d-v5 (30 agents; 3600 final episodes). title: Surrogate normal-forms for the numerical bifurcation and stability analysis of Navier-Stokes flows via machine learning
venue: Communications in Nonlinear Science and Numerical Simulation
abstract: Inspired by the Equation-Free paradigm, we propose an “embed–learn–lift” numerical framework for the solution of the inverse problem for the Navier–Stokes equations by constructing minimal-dimensional surrogate reduced oders models (ROMs). The proposed framework allows for the systematic numerical analysis, even in the presence of symmetries that standard machine-learning surrogates often fail to preserve. The framework consists of four main stages. First, manifold learning (here both Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) and Diffusion Maps (DMs)) is used to uncover the intrinsic geometry and dimensionality of the latent space underlying the high-dimensional spatio-temporal Navier–Stokes dynamics across the parameter space. In the second stage, we construct ROMs (here, via Gaussian Process regression (GPR)) of minimal dimension—by learning the evolution equations directly on the latent space identified in the first stage. In the third stage, we exploit the toolkit of numerical bifurcation analysis (here MATCONT) to construct bifurcation diagrams and perform systematic stability analysis directly in the latent coordinates. This enables, for example, the efficient continuation of branches of limit cycles emerging from Andronov–Hopf and Neimark–Sacker bifurcations, including the continuation of stable and unstable limit cycles, together with the computation of their periods and stability properties via Floquet multipliers. Such analysis is effectively intractable for the full Navier–Stokes equations. Finally, by solving the pre-image problem in manifold learning, we reconstruct the bifurcating steady and time-periodic states in the original high-dimensional physical space, thus closing the “lift” step of the pipeline. The effectiveness of the proposed methodology is demonstrated on three benchmark two-dimensional configurations: the wake flow past a circular cylinder, the planar sudden-expansion channel flow, and the fluidic pinball. As the Reynolds number Re increases, these systems exhibit Andronov–Hopf, pitchfork (symmetry-breaking), and Neimark–Sacker bifurcations, respectively. We show that DMs-based ROMs allow for a computationally efficient and accurate numerical bifurcation and stability analysis, thus outperforming the widely used POD-ROMs by providing a geometrically consistent parametrization and correctly identifying the intrinsic dimension even in the presence of secondary instabilities, highlighting the need for nonlinear manifold learning methods in CFD.

title: Physics-informed LSTM for ridge bifurcation prediction in lithium niobate crystal growth
abstract: In the Czochralski growth of lithium niobate, early identification of growth-ridge bifurcation before operator intervention is essential for supporting timely process adjustment and improving yield. This paper proposes a bifurcation risk prediction method that integrates causal temporal encoding with physics-guided temporal attention. Shallow features, including statistical descriptors, tracking errors, differences, and change rates, are first extracted from industrial production data and refined using variance and correlation-based feature selection. A causally padded TCN–GRU temporal encoder is then used to compress the selected features into a compact latent sequence while preserving historical temporal dependencies. Based on this representation, a physics-informed LSTM introduces process-physics-guided variables into the temporal attention mechanism to emphasize bifurcation-relevant time windows and suppress disturbance-related fluctuations. Experiments on real manufacturing data show that the proposed method outperforms representative baselines, including TCN, GRU, and LSTM. On the same-furnace internal test set, it achieves a precision of 86.79% and a recall of 95.11%. Cross-furnace evaluations on four independent furnace runs further demonstrate stable generalization, with event-level warning lead times ranging from 8.0 to 11.0 min for detected bifurcation events.

title: A hierarchical SINDy identification method for high-codimension bifurcations based on dynamical bifurcation theory and structural dictionary design
abstract: To reveal the inherent dynamics of high-codimensional bifurcation systems, this paper proposes a hierarchical sparse-identification framework guided by bifurcation theory and structural dictionary design. The method combines transient and attractor information within a weighted optimization framework to identify reduced dynamical models of complex nonlinear systems. Compared with standard sparse-regression formulations based directly on derivative estimation, the proposed approach uses an integral-form data representation together with elastic-net regularization to improve robustness against noise and ill-conditioning. In the numerical examples reported here, sparse identification is performed on theory-guided reduced coordinates obtained from center-subspace projection or amplitude/slow-flow reduction, keeping the identified reduced models directly comparable with reduced equations available in the literature.Numerical experiments on a delayed Liénard equation, a van der Pol–Duffing oscillator with delayed feedback, and a ship-roll model with time-delay control indicate that the proposed framework can identify reduced models that are compatible with the local Hopf-type regime structure and can estimate low-dimensional amplitude equations associated with double-Hopf behavior under noisy conditions. In addition, a synchronized cell-free genetic-clock example shows that the same hierarchical identification philosophy can be adapted to a discrete peak-to-peak return-map setting. Overall, the proposed framework provides a practical route for data-driven reduced-order modeling of bifurcation-dominated systems while highlighting the importance of data preprocessing, structural prior information, and matching the identification target to the available reduced coordinates.

title: Bifurcation potential fields for resilience analysis in dynamical systems
abstract: Bifurcation Potential Fields (VB fields) provide a compact, field-theoretic representation of stability margins across parameter space in nonlinear dynamical systems, capturing a key geometric component of resilience. Defined as scalar fields over bifurcation geometry, VB fields synthesize phase-space structure with the number and stability of equilibria under parametric change. We apply this framework to a progression of canonical (normal-form) and mechanistic (physical and ecological) models, demonstrating how stability margins can be quantified and compared across systems with differing bifurcation organization. Across these systems, we identify stability–margin discontinuities: discrete changes in distance to collapse arising from bifurcation-induced transitions in the equilibrium that defines the stability boundary. We further highlight conceptual axes along which VB fields vary, including stability architecture, dimensionality (1D vs. 2D), symmetry, phase-space folding, and structural realism. These axes shape the location of collapse thresholds, the geometry of collapse pathways and the interpretation of collapse risk. This approach generalizes across canonical and mechanistic one- and two-dimensional model classes, offering a unified geometric framework for quantifying vulnerability to both state-space perturbations and parameter drift.

title: Sparse Identification for bifurcating phenomena in Computational Fluid Dynamics
abstract: This work investigates model reduction techniques for nonlinear parameterized and time-dependent PDEs, specifically focusing on bifurcating phenomena in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). We develop interpretable and non-intrusive Reduced Order Models (ROMs) capable of capturing dynamics associated with bifurcations by identifying a minimal set of coordinates. Our methodology combines the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method with a deep learning framework based on Autoencoder (AE) architectures. To enhance dimensionality reduction, we integrate a nested Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) with the SINDy-AE architecture, enabling a sparse discovery of system dynamics while maintaining efficiency of the reduced model. We demonstrate our approach via two challenging test cases defined on sudden-expansion channel geometries: a symmetry-breaking bifurcation and a Hopf bifurcation. Starting from a comprehensive analysis of their high-fidelity behavior, i.e. symmetry-breaking phenomena and the rise of unsteady periodic solutions, we validate the accuracy and computational efficiency of our ROMs. The results show successful reconstruction of the bifurcations, accurate prediction of system evolution for unseen parameter values, and significant speed-up compared to full-order methods.

title: Nonlinear oscillations in ride-hailing rebalancing with delays and congestion
abstract: Ride-hailing platforms rebalance idle vehicles using demand and supply information that is often delayed by sensing, prediction, and implementation. Such delays may turn corrective rebalancing into phase-lagged feedback, causing persistent oscillations in regional queues and idle-vehicle stocks. This paper develops a parsimonious two-region macroscopic delay differential model that couples passenger accumulation, congestion-sensitive matching, delayed service completion, and delayed empty-vehicle rebalancing. The model yields explicit feasibility conditions for the symmetric equilibrium and a delay-dependent characteristic equation for the antisymmetric imbalance mode. Linear stability analysis shows that information latency, rebalancing travel time, service delay, and rebalancing gain can induce a Hopf bifurcation, through which the balanced operating point loses stability. Weakly nonlinear analysis and simulations further show that smooth rebalancing and saturating matching limit amplitude growth and support stable periodic oscillations. The results identify interpretable stability levers for ride-hailing operations, including latency reduction, gain moderation, service-time control, and congestion-aware rebalancing.

title: Modeling of oscillating heat pipes: Equilibria, stagnation, startup, bifurcation, oscillation, conductance, and statistics
abstract: A reduced-order model has been developed to describe the nonlinear dynamics of oscillating heat pipes (OHPs). Its formulation consists of two first-order ordinary differential equations for momentum balance and one for the net rate of evaporation and condensation, yielding three equations per liquid-slug/vapor-plug pair. The model captures key aspects of OHP behavior, including equilibrium, stagnation, startup, bifurcation, oscillation, and thermal conductance. With fixed system parameters, the model’s dynamics depend in a complex manner on initial conditions, necessitating statistical averaging to determine thermal conductance. The model’s relative simplicity reduces computational overhead, permitting hundreds to thousands of simulation runs on a supercomputer to compute averages with 95% Z-confidence intervals, allowing statistically meaningful conclusions. The dependence of total thermal conductance — incorporating both latent and sensible heat effects — on temperature difference, number of slug-plug pairs, fill fraction, and number of turns is examined. Using the framework of nonlinear dynamics, we explain bifurcation phenomena, stopovers, multiple attractors, and transitions among attractors. These statistical analyses of large-scale simulations provide a new basis for the design and optimization of OHP performance.

title: Modeling tumor-immune interactions with hyper-allee effects: Formulation, stability, and bifurcation analysis
abstract: Cancer progression emerges from a dynamical interplay between neoplastic growth and immune surveillance, yet most mathematical models reduce this interaction to logistic kinetics or single-threshold Allee effects, overlooking the layered barrier structure that governs tumor establishment. We introduce a three-dimensional immuno-oncology model coupling immune effector cells, cancer cells, and immunotherapy, which we reduce via singular perturbation and scale to a dimensionless planar system. The key novelty lies in endowing both compartments with generalized Allee functions: a single threshold for immune recruitment and a dual hyper-Allee law for tumor growth, reflecting cooperative, autocrine, and threshold-dependent processes at low cell densities. Through bifurcation analysis and numerical continuation in the clinically motivated parameter plane of immune loss versus cytotoxic efficacy, we uncover a global atlas of qualitatively distinct regimes. The organizing center is a cusp-type degenerate Bogdanov-Takens bifurcation of codimension three, from which saddle-node, Hopf, homoclinic, and limit-point-of-cycle curves emanate. Our results provide a quantitative scaffold for the three Es of cancer immunoediting: elimination, equilibrium, and escape, and suggest that patient stratification and therapeutic timing should be viewed as navigation problems in a high-dimensional threshold landscape.

title: Period-doubling route to chaos in Pulsating Heat Pipes through bifurcation and lyapunov spectrum analyses
venue: International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer
abstract: Pulsating Heat Pipes (PHPs) exhibit chaotic thermo-hydrodynamic behavior arising from the coupling of phase change, pressure oscillations, and frictional effects. This study explores the route to chaos in a simplified three-dimensional autonomous model of a PHP, governed by phase change and friction coefficients. A period-doubling cascade leading to chaos is identified through bifurcation analysis and validated by Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Lyapunov spectrum. The transition is traced through successive oscillatory regimes—first doubling from two to four, then to eight, and eventually becoming chaotic—capturing the classical period-doubling route. At each bifurcation, the second Lyapunov exponent touches zero, revealing a one-to-one correspondence between bifurcation points and dynamical instability. The dissipative behavior of the system is characterized through its divergence, analytically proportional to a friction parameter representing viscous-like damping. This damping term, embedded in the momentum equation, acts as a continuous energy sink that extracts kinetic energy from oscillatory motion and dissipates it as heat. The sum of Lyapunov exponents, calculated using the Wolf algorithm, matches the divergence of the vector field, highlighting the intrinsic link between energy dissipation and trajectory divergence in phase space. The universality of the transition is supported by the calculated Feigenbaum constant, which converges to ≈4.6692. These findings offer a deeper understanding of nonlinear dynamics and dissipation in PHPs, providing a theoretical foundation for future control and optimization of chaotic oscillations in thermal systems.

title: Parameter-aware photonic reservoir computing: Robust prediction against driving laser bifurcation drift
abstract: Traditional photonic reservoir computing (PRC) suffers from a critical bottleneck: static parameter configurations fail to adapt to nonlinear dynamic changes induced by bifurcation parameter drift, causing severe accuracy degradation and impeding the transition from laboratory research to engineering applications. To address this issue, we propose and experimentally validate a parameter-aware photonic reservoir computer (PA-PRC) based on a distributed feedback (DFB) laser with optical injection and delayed optical feedback, which achieves robust prediction under driving laser feedback strength drift. The core mechanism is a linear mapping from the bifurcation parameter to the reservoir laser's bias current via a modular controller, which explicitly embeds parameter information into reservoir dynamics for adaptive tracking of input nonlinear evolution. Using six chaotic signal sets under distinct feedback strengths, we train a single output weight matrix with only three sets. Both simulations and hardware experiments demonstrate that the one-step-ahead prediction normalized mean square errors (NMSEs) of all six sets (including three untrained sets) are below 0.1, enabling strong generalization to unseen parameters without retraining or hardware reconfiguration. The parameter-aware mechanism effectively mitigates the static-dynamic mismatch in conventional PRC, providing a feasible solution for real-time photonic signal processing applications such as high-precision parameter estimation and inter-symbol interference compensation in high-speed optical networks.

title: Bifurcation-coded memory: A novel parameter-space framework for neural information storage
abstract: We introduce Bifurcation-Coded Memory (BCM), a fundamentally new associative memory paradigm that stores memories as qualitatively distinct regions in the bifurcation parameter space of a low-dimensional dynamical system, rather than as fixed-point attractors in neural activity space. This shift—from where the system settles to how the system behaves—yields exponential capacity scaling: C=(2R/δ)m memories for m-dimensional control, compared with the linear (0.14N) and polynomial limits of classical and modern Hopfield networks. We prove three core theorems (geometric capacity bound, exponential scaling, topological noise protection) and a new partial-cue robustness result (Proposition 4) formalising the minimum information retention threshold for reliable recall. Controlled synthetic experiments confirm the scaling predictions: 62.2% accuracy with 1D pitchfork bifurcations, 85.7% with 2D Wilson-Cowan dynamics, and 100% retrieval of 40 memories in 3D control space. On MNIST (60,000 samples), BA-VAE-BCM achieves 95.21 ± 0.49% with 392:1 compression, significantly outperforming Modern Hopfield Networks (91.6 ± 0.1%, p<0.001). Cross-species biological validation through BCM-Encoder—a discriminative variant preserving the 2D parameter-space readout—demonstrates broad applicability: 98.30% on C. elegans binary navigation, 93.38% on macaque 4-class motor decoding, and 30.05% on 40-class human EEG visual decoding (4.43× over Hopfield, 5.51× over ESN), with BCM's advantage growing systematically with task complexity.

title: Graph-guided generative oversampling via latent manifold representation for imbalanced data
abstract: In risk-averse operational environments, such as financial fraud detection and medical screening, decision support systems face the critical challenge of asymmetric misclassification costs. While identifying minority crisis events is paramount, over-allocating operational resources to false positives drastically increases verification costs and induces alert fatigue, ultimately eroding the system's trustworthiness. Traditional data-level resampling methods often ignore the underlying nonlinear topological manifold of high-dimensional data, leading to linear piercing and classification noise. Meanwhile, existing deep generative models often suffer from mode collapse and a "high recall, low precision" dilemma when facing extremely scarce minority classes. To address these challenges, this paper proposes G3O (Graph-Guided Generative Oversampling), a framework that decouples resampling spatial positioning and feature generation. First, it accurately locates high-value boundary seeds using a global k-nearest neighbor graph and local imbalance factor (LIF), avoiding ineffective sampling in safe and noise regions. Second, it introduces a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) to extract the denoised intrinsic manifold, performing interpolation in the compact latent space with superimposed isotropic smooth perturbations. This mechanism expands minority class diversity at the decision boundary while strictly adhering to semantic validity. Large-scale Monte Carlo evaluations on 11 high-difficulty datasets across general, financial, and medical fields validate the framework. Results show that as a robust preprocessing engine, G3O seamlessly empowers domain benchmark algorithms (e.g., CS-GBM, RUSBoost), achieving statistically significant performance improvements in PR-AUC and F1-Score. This study provides a theoretically complete and generalizable paradigm for extreme skew distribution problems in high-risk scenarios.

title: Geometry-informed bifurcation type identification via Zernike moments
abstract: Identifying bifurcation types from data is challenging when the governing equations are unknown and the available observations are noisy, sparse, or ordered by perturbation conditions rather than by continuous time. We introduce a geometry-informed framework that maps condition-ordered one-dimensional observations into lag-coordinate point clouds, converts them into two-dimensional (2D) histogram images, and extracts compact Zernike-moment descriptors for supervised machine-learning classification. The training set is generated from stochastic realizations of canonical normal forms for fold, transcritical, pitchfork, and Hopf bifurcations, together with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU)-type neutral baseline. Using K-nearest neighbors (KNN) as a transparent baseline classifier, the method achieves remarkably high accuracy on the standard-form benchmark. The remaining errors are confined mainly to the Hopf-neutral boundary. Additional classifier comparisons confirm that the discriminative information is primarily encoded in the Zernike descriptors rather than in a specific classifier choice. We further examine generalization using a mechanistic gene-regulatory model, the genetic toggle switch, whose pre-jump segments are consistently assigned to the fold class, in agreement with its known fold-type transition. Finally, when applied to a real single-cell epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) dataset organized along an experimental dose axis, the framework shows that mesenchymal and composite EMT coordinates generate stable fold-like signatures under bootstrap voting, and several core genes reproduce the same pattern. These results indicate that moment-based geometric representations provide an interpretable and transferable route for bifurcation type identification in synthetic, mechanistic, and real biological systems.

title: Data-driven joint representation and prediction of nonlinear dynamical systems from unlabeled trajectories
venue: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering
abstract: The task of jointly forecasting dynamical systems from unlabeled, trajectory-varying measurements is confronted by a fundamental circular dependency: identifying system parameters requires known equations, while modeling equations presupposes estimated parameters. A dual-network Joint Representation And Prediction (JoRAP) framework is proposed to resolve this interdependence, simultaneously distinguishing all trajectories and approximating their vector fields. JoRAP integrates a trajectory representation neural network (TRNN) that encodes individual trajectories into vectorial embeddings, and a vector field neural network (VFNN) that infers the derivatives at any states from each embedding. This co-design enables a fully autonomous learning, simultaneously identifying diverse trajectories and capturing the characteristics of dynamical behaviors. Evaluated on unlabeled trajectories of nonlinear dynamical systems with partial observability, JoRAP achieves accurate long-horizon predictions and learns representations that distinguish dynamical regimes such as periodic, chaotic, and multistable behaviors. Our framework establishes a data-driven paradigm that requires neither predefined equations nor known parameters, enabling joint analysis and forecast of diverse complex systems from observations alone.

title: Physically interpretable representation learning with Gaussian Mixture Variational AutoEncoder (GM-VAE)
venue: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering
abstract: Extracting compact, physically interpretable representations from high-dimensional scientific data is a persistent challenge due to the complex, nonlinear structures inherent in physical systems. Unlike conventional VAEs that jointly optimize reconstruction and clustering (often leading to training instability), our method utilizes a block-coordinate descent strategy, alternating between expectation and maximization steps. To objectively evaluate the learned representations, we introduce a quantitative metric based on graph-Laplacian smoothness, which measures the coherence of physical quantities across the latent manifold. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework on datasets of increasing complexity: surface reaction ODEs, Navier–Stokes wake flows, and experimental laser-induced combustion Schlieren images. title: GALDS: A graph-autoencoder-based latent dynamics surrogate model to predict neurite material transport
venue: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering
abstract: Neurons exhibit intricate geometries within their neurite networks, which play a crucial role in processes such as signaling and nutrient transport. Accurate simulation of material transport in the networks is essential for understanding these biological phenomena but poses significant computational challenges because of the complex tree-like structures involved. Traditional approaches are time-intensive and resource-demanding, yet the inherent properties of neuron trees, which consists primarily of pipes with steady-state parabolic velocity profiles and bifurcations, provide opportunities for computational optimization. To address these challenges, we propose a Graph-Autoencoder-based Latent Dynamics Surrogate (GALDS) model, which is specifically designed to streamline the simulation of material transport in neural trees. GALDS employs a graph autoencoder to encode latent representations of the network's geometry, velocity fields, and concentration profiles. These latent space representations are then assembled into a global graph, which is subsequently used to predict system dynamics in the latent space via a trained graph latent space system dynamic model, inspired by the Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) concept. The integration of an autoencoder allows for the use of smaller graph neural network models with reduced training data requirements. Furthermore, the Neural ODE component effectively mitigates the issue of error accumulation commonly encountered in recurrent neural networks. The effectiveness of the GALDS model is demonstrated through results on eight unseen geometries and four abnormal transport examples, where our approach achieves mean relative error of 3% with maximum relative error <8% and demonstrates a 10-fold speed improvement compared to previous surrogate model approaches.

title: Generative learning for slow manifolds and bifurcation diagrams
abstract: In dynamical systems characterized by separation of time scales, the approximation of so called “slow manifolds”, on which the long term dynamics lie, is a useful step for model reduction. Initializing on such slow manifolds is a useful step in modeling, since it circumvents fast transients, and is crucial in multiscale algorithms (like the equation-free approach) alternating between fine scale (fast) and coarser scale (slow) simulations. In a similar spirit, when one studies the infinite time dynamics of systems depending on parameters, the system attractors (e.g., its steady states) lie on bifurcation diagrams (curves for one-parameter continuation, and more generally, on manifolds in state × parameter space. Sampling these manifolds gives us representative attractors (here, steady states of ODEs or PDEs) at different parameter values. Algorithms for the systematic construction of these manifolds (slow manifolds, bifurcation diagrams) are required parts of the “traditional” numerical nonlinear dynamics toolkit. In more recent years, as the field of Machine Learning develops, conditional score-based generative models (cSGMs) have been demonstrated to exhibit remarkable capabilities in generating plausible data from target distributions that are conditioned on some given label. It is tempting to exploit such generative models to produce samples of data distributions (points on a slow manifold, steady states on a bifurcation surface) conditioned on (consistent with) some quantity of interest (QoI, observable). In this work, we present a framework for using cSGMs to quickly (a) initialize on a low-dimensional (reduced-order) slow manifold of a multi-time-scale system consistent with desired value(s) of a QoI (a “label”) on the manifold, and (b) approximate steady states in a bifurcation diagram consistent with a (new, out-of-sample) parameter value. This conditional sampling can help uncover the geometry of the reduced slow-manifold and/or approximately “fill in” missing segments of steady states in a bifurcation diagram. The quantity of interest, which determines how the sampling is conditioned, is either known a priori or identified using manifold learning-based dimensionality reduction techniques applied to the training data.

title: Piezoelectric air actuators for electronic thermal management: a bibliometric and comprehensive review
abstract: With the continuous rise in heat flux density in high-power electronic devices, conventional cooling strategies increasingly struggle to achieve an effective balance among system footprint, noise, energy consumption, and heat transfer performance. Piezoelectric air actuators have therefore emerged as a promising active air-cooling technology for electronic thermal management. This review examines 660 relevant publications indexed in the Web of Science from 2000 to 2026, identified through topic-based screening and citation tracing. The bibliometric analysis systematically examines the field's developmental trajectory, research collaboration networks, and evolving research hotspots. The technical analysis also comprehensively and critically examines the structural evolution, flow mechanisms, and heat transfer characteristics of cantilever-type piezoelectric fans, zero-net-mass-flux piezoelectric synthetic jet actuators, and non-zero-net-mass-flux piezoelectric synthetic jet actuators. A complete energy-transfer chain from electrical input to heat removal is established, and a multidimensional evaluation framework integrating flow, thermal, and acoustic performance is further proposed. By linking academic advances with industrial practice, this review indicates that ultrasonic-frequency piezoelectric synthetic jet actuators may offer application-specific advantages for high-heat-flux, low-noise, thin, array-scalable, and embedded electronic cooling systems. Finally, current limitations include insufficient understanding of multiphysics coupling, inadequate system-level evaluation criteria, limited array coordination, and inadequate operational stability. Commercialization is further constrained by manufacturing repeatability and system-level competitiveness. Future research should prioritize energy efficiency, long-term reliability, and versatile applicability, providing theoretical guidance for the development of compact piezoelectric active air-cooling technologies.

title: Conventional and additive manufacturing of NiTi shape memory alloy tubes: A review of fabrication, multiaxial thermomechanical behavior, constitutive modeling, and emerging applications in actuation and elastocaloric cooling
abstract: This review critically assesses the state of research on NiTi shape memory alloy tubes fabricated via both conventional thermomechanical processing and additive manufacturing (AM), with emphasis on Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF). Synthesizing over 157 studies on fabrication, multiaxial thermomechanical characterization, constitutive modeling, and applications in actuation and elastocaloric cooling, this work addresses the full lifecycle of NiTi tubes from processing to performance. Unlike prior reviews that treat AM fabrication or constitutive modeling of NiTi independently, this review integrates, for thin-walled tubular geometries specifically, fabrication-induced microstructure, multiaxial thermomechanical characterization, constitutive model validation, and application performance in a single treatment, a combination not addressed collectively by any prior review in this domain. Experiments under uniaxial tension, pure torsion, and proportional and non-proportional axial-torsional loading reveal significant tension-torsion coupling, rate-dependent transformations, and pronounced anisotropy in drawn tubes. A microplane-based constitutive model, validated against these experiments with a maximum error of 3.3%, effectively captures superelasticity and shape memory behavior across all loading paths. For LPBF-fabricated tubes, the review examines the influence of post-processing on transformation temperatures, strain localization, cyclic stability, and wall thickness effects, demonstrating that optimized heat treatment yields recoverable strains approaching those of wrought material. The analysis identifies four prioritized research gaps: (i) scarce multiaxial fatigue data for LPBF tubes, (ii) insufficient incorporation of AM-induced microstructural variability into constitutive models, (iii) the lack of standardized protocols for comparing conventional and AM tube performance, and (iv) limited integration of data-driven and machine learning methods with physics-based models for predictive design. A research roadmap is proposed, emphasizing manufacturing-aware models, LPBF-specific multiaxial datasets, and data-driven approaches to accelerate the translation of NiTi tubes into reliable engineering devices.

title: Sensor-actuator integration in intelligent devices: from functional synergy to emerging application
abstract: The integration of sensors and actuators in intelligent devices has led to the revolutionary change in the fields of robotics, healthcare, and IoT to allow the perception-to-action cycles. This interactions leads to real-time responsiveness, flexibility, and autonomy, and creates innovations, including soft robotics, bioelectronic medicine, and smart wearable devices. However, there are still problems associated with the attainment of signal coordination control, miniaturization and strong interoperability in dynamic environments. This paper reviews the design principles of sensor-actuator integration, highlighting key mechanisms for functional synergy, such as feedback architectures, multimodal sensing, and adaptive actuation. The emerging applications, including soft robotics and human-machine interfaces are then examined, with an emphasis on how cross-disciplinary solutions are tackling the existing constraints. Finally, we discuss the directions of the future, such as biohybrid systems and neuromorphic engineering, which are projected to restructure the limits of intelligent devices. By synthesizing theoretical insights with practical advancements, this work is expected to help the researchers overcome the existing limitations and open the opportunities of this rapidly evolving field.

title: Discrete-state photomechanical actuators
abstract: Directly transducing light into work is attractive for remotely powering soft mechanisms designed from photoresponsive polymers, but presents challenges for achieving reliable actuation within a control framework. Here, we utilize azobenzene-functionalized polyimides to fabricate actuators characterized by mechanically discrete states. Irradiation initiates the photochemically induced, quasistatic deformation to advance the actuator to the edge of instability. Following this latency, ultrafast snap through actuation (∼10 ms-scale) ensues. Restricting the role of control to the attainment of the edge of instability, strategies for achieving repetitive actuation via multiplexed irradiation are demonstrated. Approaches are examined for modulating the latency of the actuator using an all-optical strategy as well as mechanical design of the actuator. Prototypical assemblies of these actuators in arrays are used to fabricate morphable surfaces and structures, which is aided by the realization that the ultrafast actuation is characterized by a high power-density on the order of ∼kW/m3.

title: Sensor and actuator integrated tooling systems
abstract: The advances in electronics, sensors, actuators, smart materials, computers, and communication technologies led to new and improved mechatronics-based smart tooling systems. This paper reviews the sensors and actuators used in tooling systems. The sensor principles to measure force, displacement, and temperature are explained. Actuators based on piezo, magnetorheological fluid, shape memory alloy, and magnetostrictive principles are discussed. Wireless and wire-based power supply and signal transmission techniques to stationary and rotating tools are described. The integration of sensors, actuators, power supply, and microcontrollers to various tooling systems used in boring, milling, turning, and grinding operations are presented along with their process monitoring and control applications in the industry. It is shown that the sensor-actuator tooling systems improve the accuracy, robustness, and productivity of machining which adds intelligence to the machine tools. The current challenges include widening the operating bandwidth of tooling systems, wireless power and high-speed data transmission, miniaturization of actuators and sensors, and onboard processing using embedded micro-controllers.

title: Phase change materials in space systems. Fundamental applications, materials and special requirements – A review
abstract: Thermal control is a critical functionality in space applications due to the narrow operation temperature range of the on-board systems, and, on the other hand, due to the harsh environment the spacecraft is subject to. Thermal control systems based on phase change materials have the main advantage that are passive and, if properly designed, are highly reliable and efficient. Some Phase Change Materials (PCMs) – paraffins – have other applications for spacecrafts, such as mechanical actuators, which convert temperature changes to mechanical work. In contrast to thermal control terrestrial applications, space applications have more constraints and must ensure compatibility with more systems. One of the most important constraints in space systems is the mass. The design and choice of thermal regulation systems often boils down to replacing heat dissipation radiators mass with lighter, PCM elements. The review is centered around the main application area of PCMs in space applications, discussing numerical and experimental studies on the design and multi-objective optimization of thermal control systems for spacecrafts. Other PCM applications in spacecraft technology are discussed such as micro-actuators, thermoelectric devices, propulsion systems and thermal protection for reentry vehicles. Not only PCM applications are discussed but also some specific issues which are highly important in the design and effective operation of PCM-based thermal control systems for spacecrafts. Thus, issues such as materials, performance enhancement, stability, compatibility and phase transition process under microgravity or hyper gravity were reviewed.

title: Physics-informed reinforcement learning for energy-efficient unmanned aerial vehicle navigation with context-aware power estimation
abstract: The transition of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) from simulation to real-world deployment presents significant challenges due to the simulation-to-reality (sim-to-real) gap, particularly concerning simplified electromechanical dynamics and energy optimization. To address these discrepancies, this paper proposes a hierarchical framework integrating bottom-up physics modeling, neural system identification, and energy-aware control. In contrast to conventional kinematic models, the developed high-fidelity environment explicitly integrates actuator dynamics, including voltage saturation, Back-Electromotive Force (Back-EMF), and transient delays, ensuring that the learned policies respect realistic physical constraints. Central to this framework is a novel context-aware neural architecture designed to decouple flight states from latent hardware signatures. This module achieves a hardware classification accuracy exceeding 97% and robust power estimation with a nominal Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE) of approximately 1.5%, effectively functioning as a virtual sensor. Leveraging these learned dynamics, we introduce an Energy-Cost-Optimized Reinforcement Learning (Eco-RL) policy that couples a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) planner with a robust Feedback Linearization and Model Reference Adaptive Control (FBL-MRAC) execution layer. By incorporating the learned power consumption into the reinforcement learning reward loop, the agent synthesizes momentum-conserving trajectories that strategically trade off altitude potential against air density variations. Extensive validation across five heterogeneous hardware classes demonstrates an overall energy reduction of 19.8% across randomized sorties, which consolidates into a highly significant 13.5% efficiency gain under strict pair-wise evaluations compared to standard policies, confirming the efficacy of physics-informed Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) in optimizing flight efficiency.

title: Multi-configuration recognition of a 3-RSR parallel mechanism with zero-torsion characteristics based on screw algebra and high-order kinematics
abstract: In this paper, a comprehensive high-order kinematic analysis of a geometrically symmetric 3-RSR parallel mechanism is conducted based on screw algebra. A screw-based modeling framework is first established to represent the pose and evaluate the mobility under zero-torsion characteristics, revealing the mechanism's intrinsic 2R1T motion pattern. The bifurcation configurations of the 3-RSR mechanism under singularity are then identified, deriving five distinct motion modes: decoupled limb-swinging, parallel translation, two interfering rotational modes, and axis rotation. Eleven bifurcated motion branches are subsequently derived through high-order velocity constraints and symmetry extension. In particular, a complete symmetry-based configuration space is constructed for the first time, which enables systematic recognition and classification of multimodal motion. Moreover, the feasibility of connectivity among motion branches is verified through constraint screw evolution. These findings not only deepen the understanding of singularity-induced bifurcations in reconfigurable parallel mechanisms, but also establish the constraint principles that govern configuration transitions of reconfigurable parallel mechanisms under singular configurations.

title: Reliability-based chance-constrained control for suppressing parametric oscillations in multi-timescale gas turbine systems
abstract: Within the automatic control mode of gas turbines, ubiquitous parametric oscillations arise from periodic and stochastic operational excitations in a multi-timescale coupled nonlinear gas-path system (MN-GPS), thereby posing a severe threat to operational safety. To elucidate the formation mechanisms of these oscillations and propose a robust suppression control strategy, this study introduces a reliability-based chance-constrained control and develops a comprehensive model integrating gas-path, mechanical, and hydraulic subsystems with dead-band effects. The excitation of fuel system was extracted from operational data and incorporated into MN-GPS model, which was validated by steady-state and transient operating data under different conditions. The proportional gain under different time-scaling factors exhibits supercritical pitchfork bifurcation, and the transition between stable and extreme parametric oscillation has a step characteristic. Fast-slow timescale convergence induces extreme instability events that dramatically reduce operational reliability. Both the degree and time delay of stability margin are significantly influenced by nonlinear dead-band effects during dynamic operation process. Based on the parameter oscillation state transition law, a fast compensator based on reliability-based chance constraints was designed to suppress parameter oscillations, and its effectiveness was verified through comparisons with methods such as ADRC and LSTM-NN. The comparative simulation and Hardware-in-the-Loop testing results show that the proposed method can effectively suppress extreme oscillations under continuous excitation and maintain the system operating in a high-reliability region. This work provides solutions for parameter oscillation risk suppression and operation reliability optimization in multi-scale nonlinear industrial systems.

title: A hybrid fractional-order PID-PSO adaptive token bucket architecture for resilient IoT supply chain security
venue: Engineering Science and Technology, an International Journal
abstract: The rapid integration of Internet of Things (IoT) devices into industrial supply chains exposes embedded gateways to distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks that can destabilize latency-sensitive industrial processes. This paper introduces a hybrid Fractional-Order PID (FOPID) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) Token Bucket architecture implemented at the XDP (eXpress Data Path) native hook, the earliest programmable point in the Linux kernel. The FOPID controller dynamically adjusts the Token Bucket replenishment rate using real-time network throughput and traffic statistics, enabling proportional rate regulation that helps preserve legitimate bursty flows while mitigating malicious traffic. A trigger-driven PSO layer, activated only when stability thresholds are violated, tunes the five FOPID gains by minimizing the Integrated Time Absolute Error (ITAE) criterion. The optimized parameters are transmitted to the kernel-space FOPID controller via eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) maps, allowing low-latency control updates with limited runtime overhead. The control mechanism uses a fixed control-sampling period to support timely adaptation while maintaining the timing constraints of the target cyber-physical setting. Experimental results on a physical IoT warehouse testbed show that the proposed architecture improves both resilience and service stability under multi-vector attacks. Relative to the standard Token Bucket, the method reduced packet loss by 7.7–18.5%, and compared with iptables hashlimit, it lowered CPU utilization by 10–30%. Under Layer 7 flooding, it constrained P99 latency to 132.90 ms.

title: Ghost imaging-based lightweight encryption scheme with auxiliary probe verification for industrial inspection robots
abstract: In the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), drone-based industrial inspection robots have been widely deployed, posing significant challenges to the secure transmission of industrial vision data. This paper proposes a lightweight industrial vision encryption scheme based on computational ghost imaging (CGI) with auxiliary probe verification. First, a novel 3D memristor-modulated hyperchaotic map (3D-MMHM) is developed as the core encryption engine. Lyapunov exponent spectra, bifurcation analysis, and NIST randomness tests demonstrate that the proposed model exhibits excellent unpredictability and a large key space. Based on the 3D-MMHM, a dual-track encryption framework is constructed. The main track integrates CGI-inspired global pixel permutation with dynamically cascaded diffusion chains to enhance resistance against chosen-plaintext attacks, while the auxiliary track employs a lightweight CGI-based auxiliary probe mechanism to intercept abnormal packets prior to decryption, thereby reducing unnecessary computational overhead under channel interference. Security performance evaluations show that the NPCR and UACI values reach 99.61% and 33.46%, while the ciphertext entropy approaches 8.0. Moreover, the proposed scheme achieves an encryption throughput of up to 3578.60 KB/s for high-resolution industrial images, demonstrating strong potential for real-time visual data protection in harsh industrial environments.

title: Recent advances on performance enhancement techniques of phase change materials for energy storage system: a review
abstract: Phase change materials (PCMs) are promising mediums for high-density thermal energy storage (HTES), and have the potential to become important and useful in the fields of concentrated solar power, industrial waste heat recovery, and advanced thermal management systems. The very low thermal conductivity, however, is an intrinsic property that limits heat transfer rates and system efficiency. This review provides a critical, multi-scale synthesis of recent advances in latent heat thermal energy storage (LHTES) materials, structures, and systems, focusing on material modification, structural design, and system optimization. The major enhancement strategies are the integration of porous media (such as metal foams and expanded graphite), the incorporation of carbon-based and metal/metal oxide nanoparticles as nano-enhanced PCM, the introduction of the encapsulation technique to enhance the stability and leakage prevention, and the modification of the structure by the use of fins and heat pipes. At the system level, cascaded PCM configurations, along with active enhancement techniques such as rotation, vibration, and multi-field, are demonstrated to significantly improve heat transfer, temperature uniformity, and charging, discharging performance. The analysis uncovers key challenges and trade-offs, including nanoparticle instability, declining latent heat, the lack of widely accepted evaluation frameworks, and the need for long-term validation. It is suggested that future research should focus on application-specific, integrated design strategies, with standardized benchmarking, advanced optimization, and field validation, to facilitate the deployment of PCM-based thermal energy storage systems on a larger scale and at a lower cost.

title: Electromagnetically reshaped nonlinear stiffness through a 2-DoF X-mechanism for coupled vibration isolation
abstract: With a new concept, nonlinear reshaping, this study presents a novel electromagnetically reshaped X-structured platform, engineered to tackle the persistent challenge of adaptive vibration isolation specifically for coupled vertical–rotational excitations and variable payloads. Evolving from a previous X-mechanism, our design incorporates two pivotal modifications: released constraints at the central joint to introduce a new rotational degree of freedom (DoF), and integrated bilateral rhombic substructures coupled with a custom electromagnetic actuator. This synthesis enables combined vertical–rotational motion and provides a robust foundation for active stiffness modulation. Crucially, we demonstrate that the system's intrinsic nonlinear stiffness, which generates a tunable quasi-zero-stiffness (QZS) region, can be dynamically reshaped by the actuator's Lorentz force, bypassing the need for mechanical reconfiguration. Finite element analysis validates the actuator's linear thrust-current relationship and precise force–displacement profile. Dynamic modeling via Lagrange's equations and the harmonic balance method reveals that this electromagnetic control effectively separates closely spaced resonance peaks under complex coupled excitations. Experimental validation and comparative studies with a functional prototype confirm the platform's exceptional adaptability. For payloads varying in mass and moment of inertia both up to 100%, the system maintains a stable resonance frequency at 1.5±0.5 Hz and delivers consistent, robust vibration isolation performance. This work provides a practical and efficient solution for protecting sensitive equipment in dynamic environments, such as aerospace vehicles and precision manufacturing systems, where both the payload and the vibrational landscape are subject to significant change.

title: Benchmarking zero-shot vision-language models against supervised learning for concurrent metabolic rate and clothing insulation estimation
abstract: With individuals spending more than 85% of their time indoors, maintaining Thermal Comfort (TC) is essential for well-being and energy efficiency. While the Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) index is the standard metric, its accuracy suffers when personal factors, specifically Metabolic Rate (MET) and Clothing Insulation (CLO), are treated as constant values. Recent advances in Computer Vision (CV) offer a non-intrusive method to estimate these parameters, yet progress is hindered by the scarcity of privacy-compliant, granular real-world datasets. We introduce a novel high-fidelity synthetic dataset generated via Unreal Engine 5 (UE5), featuring 2250 video clips with expert-annotated ground truth for MET and CLO aligned with ASHRAE Standard 55. Leveraging this dataset, we present the first comprehensive benchmark comparing a specialized supervised model against state-of-the-art (SOTA) zero-shot Vision-Language Models (VLMs). We propose a modified pretrained multi-task Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture as a supervised baseline and contrast it with the flagship Gemini 3 Pro and the lightweight 2.5 Flash using a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategy. Results indicate that zero-shot Gemini 3 Pro significantly outperforms the CNN baseline in semantic accuracy, achieving Mean Absolute Errors (MAEs) of 0.31 MET and 0.021 CLO. Conversely, latency analysis identifies the multi-task CNN as the most viable option for high-frequency control loops due to its 3.93-second inference latency per clip, while Gemini 2.5 Flash provides a balanced, accessible alternative for periodic building adjustments. This study validates the utility of synthetic digital occupants for benchmarking AI models, enabling a scalable, privacy-preserving Occupant Centric Control (OCC) pipeline.

title: A scenario-driven review of multi-agent cooperation for lunar surface missions
abstract: The transition from short-term lunar sorties to sustained International Lunar Research Station calls for multi-agent cooperative systems. However, terrestrial swarm paradigms face a severe reality gap under lunar constraints in communication, SWaP, and radiation-hardened computing. This systematic review organizes lunar multi-agent research using a new operational taxonomy spanning three mission phases and a six-domain cooperative technical framework, and assesses validation readiness via an Evidence Maturity scale (L0–L4). Our evidence-weighted synthesis shows a bifurcated maturity landscape: while foundational exploration and mapping architectures have achieved L3 validation in terrestrial planetary analogs, actual lunar flight deployments (L4) remain absent, and research into construction, logistics, and maintenance is critically sparse. Our synthesis further reveals that validated systems consistently adopt hybrid modular architectures with communication-aware planning and human-on-the-loop supervision, while fully decentralized end-to-end learning paradigms remain confined to simulation. We further expose an assumption gap between algorithmic prerequisites and lunar physical reality. To narrow the sim-to-real chasm, we identify transferable methods from deep-space learning and in-orbit servicing, and propose a roadmap emphasizing communication autonomy, task self-organization, and engineering realism.

title: Design of a liquid state space model proportional–integral– derivative controller for generator oscillation suppression in power cyber-physical systems
abstract: Under short-circuit fault conditions in power cyber-physical systems, generator oscillations pose a serious threat to safe and stable operation. This study proposes a hybrid controller—the Liquid State Space Model Proportional–Integral–Derivative controller—that integrates a Liquid State Space Model with conventional Proportional–Integral–Derivative control. By selecting suitable state matrices to represent the controlled plant's state information, the Liquid State Space Model produces effective parameter updates for the Proportional–Integral–Derivative controller. Leveraging the Liquid State Space Model's ability to handle sequential data and to dynamically adjust its state transition matrix, the proposed controller enables real-time adaptive tuning of Proportional–Integral–Derivative gains. We apply the Liquid State Space Model Proportional–Integral–Derivative controller to a Single Machine Infinite Bus power cyber-physical system. Simulation experiments evaluate its ability to suppress generator oscillations, benchmarked against a Backpropagation Neural Network Proportional–Integral–Derivative controller, a Recurrent Neural Network Proportional–Integral–Derivative controller, and a no-controller baseline, under short-circuit faults and communication-layer network interference. For example, under a three-phase short-circuit fault with a 2-ms disturbance, the Liquid State Space Model Proportional–Integral–Derivative controller achieves an overshoot of 1.154079, outperforming the Backpropagation Neural Network Proportional–Integral–Derivative (3.294508) and the Recurrent Neural Network Proportional–Integral–Derivative (1.504131) and delivering the best overall control performance among the tested methods. Overall, results show that the Liquid State Space Model Proportional–Integral–Derivative controller provides stronger oscillation suppression and faster recovery across all tested conditions, confirming its effectiveness for complex dynamic systems.

title: Fog-Quant: A quantum computing inspired framework for fog computing deployment over 6G radio access networks
abstract: Future 6G networks promise revolutionary capabilities with terabit speeds and sub-millisecond latency. However, achieving these goals requires fundamental changes in how we manage computing resources. Traditional cloud architectures cannot meet 6G's strict timing requirements because data must travel too far to distant servers. Fog computing brings processing power closer to users by embedding micro data centers in cell towers and street infrastructure. Yet current fog orchestration methods struggle with 6G's unique challenges. Terahertz frequencies suffer severe signal degradation. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces need constant adjustment as users move. Managing thousands of diverse fog nodes while optimizing latency, energy, and resource usage becomes impossibly complex for classical algorithms. This paper introduces Fog-Quant, the first quantum-powered orchestration system designed specifically for 6G fog networks. Our framework combines two quantum algorithms to solve placement problems that defeat traditional methods. Quantum Annealing rapidly explores millions of possible solutions in microseconds. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm then refines these solutions with mathematical precision. Fog-Quant uses intelligent entropy-based decision making. Simple placement choices use fast classical methods. Complex scenarios activate quantum processing. This adaptive approach ensures optimal performance without wasting computational resources. We evaluated Fog Quant on a calibrated emulation testbed with 10,000 fog nodes and 10,000 microservices. Fog Quant reaches 96.1 percent placement success at 10,000 nodes and reduces energy use by 28.8 percent versus classical baselines. It maintains reliability above 99.995 percent with up to 30 percent node unavailability. Over 90 percent of control loop events finish within 2.2 ms, with a 2.16 ms decision time bound, meeting a 10 ms URLLC requirement in dense urban scenarios.

title: Robust multimodal latent repair for fault-tolerant cyber–physical production systems
abstract: Multimodal fusion systems in industrial environments are critically vulnerable to sensor faults that destabilize downstream tasks. In capital-intensive sectors such as automotive manufacturing and aerospace, these unmitigated failures translate directly into substantial financial losses due to unplanned downtime and catastrophic equipment damage. To address this, we introduce a mathematically grounded framework for robust multimodal latent repair, which fundamentally re-engineers the Transformer block for fault tolerance. We derive a spectral decomposition proving that residual connections preserve fault locality while attention heads diffuse it. Leveraging this orthogonality, we propose the residual-contrastive attention module. This mechanism utilizes a novel local–global ratio to explicitly detect anomalies and employs an inverse-residual gate to suppress and inpaint corrupted tokens using global context. Validated on rigorous industrial digital twins, our model-based approach achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity, providing a deterministic architectural guarantee of error containment that effectively decouples physical sensor degradation from operational system stability without relying on implicit regularization.

title: High-performance fixed-time active fault-tolerant control for robotic manipulators via sparse physics-informed dynamics learning
abstract: High-precision tracking of robotic manipulators is challenged by nonlinear friction, model mismatch, external disturbances, and abrupt actuator faults. Conventional robust controllers often lump these effects into a single uncertainty, resulting in conservative gains and high control effort. This paper develops a novel fixed-time active fault-tolerant control (AFTC) framework that couples sparse physics-informed dynamics learning with fixed-time robust compensation. A physics-informed neural network with sparse regression (PINN–SR) learns the physics gap between the nominal model and the plant and identifies parsimonious, interpretable terms for friction and structured uncertainties. A fixed-time fault observer then reconstructs the remaining lumped perturbations, including actuator faults, disturbances, and residual approximation errors. Using these compensations, a novel nonsingular fixed-time sliding-mode controller with a state-dependent exponent and hyperbolic-secant gain guarantees convergence within a settling-time bound independent of initial conditions; fixed-time stability is proven via Lyapunov analysis. MATLAB/Simulink–Simscape simulations of a 3-DOF SAMSUNG FARA AT2 manipulator against five recent controllers show improved performance. In the fault-free case, convergence time is 0.276–0.322 s, and the integral absolute error is 0.0186–0.0506rad (38–42% and approximately 40% improvements over the best baseline results, respectively). Under actuator faults, the proposed method further reduces the tracking error by 41–51% while preserving smooth control inputs.

title: Nonlinear bidirectional dynamic latent modeling for closed-loop process monitoring
abstract: Closed-loop control brings new challenges for process monitoring. Nonlinearities in the correlation structure and the dynamic relations in closed-loop process data further complicate the task. To tackle these issues, a new dynamic latent variable scheme is proposed in this paper for nonlinear closed-loop processes. The nonlinearities of the processes are investigated in detail first, followed by a dynamic latent variable object for latent structure extraction of nonlinear closed-loop processes. An algorithm is then proposed to solve the constructed optimization object which has guaranteed convergency. The relations of the extracted dynamic latent model are revealed in detail afterwards, and the process monitoring strategy is built with comprehensive analysis of variations in closed-loop process data. A numerical simulation and a study on the thruster system of the “Jiaolong” deep-sea submarine are carried on to show the performance of the proposed scheme.

title: Learning-based fault-tolerant control for flexible joint robotic manipulators: An actor-critic framework with experimental verification
abstract: Flexible-joint robotic manipulators (FJRMs) offer significant advantages over traditional rigid-link counterparts, including improved dexterity, greater motion flexibility, and lower energy consumption. However, their control remains challenging due to inherent nonlinear dynamics, elastic joint coupling, external disturbances, and susceptibility to actuator faults. This paper presents a Lyapunov-guided actor-critic reinforcement learning (RL) fault-tolerant control strategy for FJRMs. Different from conventional adaptive neural-network control, where the neural network is mainly used as a direct uncertainty approximator, the proposed method introduces a critic network to learn the long-run cost-to-go from tracking error, control effort, and fault-induced performance degradation, and uses this critic evaluation to guide actor policy improvement online. The Lyapunov design supplies a stabilizing control structure, while the actor-critic learning mechanism provides value-based policy adaptation under unknown matched uncertainties and actuator faults. Semi-global uniform ultimate boundedness of all closed-loop signals is established, and experiments on a Baxter robotic platform demonstrate improved tracking accuracy and robustness compared with PID and single neural-network controllers under faulty conditions.

title: Adaptive dynamic programming-based fault tolerant control for nonlinear time-delay systems
abstract: This study introduces a fault compensation control approach for a class of affine nonlinear time-delay systems using adaptive dynamic programming (ADP). By establishing an observer, the ADP-derived approach facilitates the estimation of potential actuator faults within the system. A novel value function is devised to incorporate the estimated fault and state delay. Subsequently, the control laws are derived from this innovative value function. The Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation associated with this innovative value function is effectively solved using a critic neural network. Then, it is demonstrated through Lyapunov theory that the closed-loop systems achieve uniform ultimate boundedness. The efficacy of the current fault compensation strategy is validated through simulation instances. A notable contribution of the proposed method is its extension of the ADP technique to address the challenge of fault compensation in nonlinear time-delay systems.

title: KPCA digital twin-enhanced real-time fault-tolerant control for autonomous vehicles
abstract: Fault-tolerant control for autonomous vehicles is challenged by sensor degradation, actuator failures, and the need for real-time fault reconstruction without interrupting operation. This paper proposes an integrated framework combining Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA) digital twin technology with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to enable unified fault detection, estimation, and real-time reconstruction. The KPCA digital twin uses kernel-based nonlinear dimensionality reduction to model complex fault dynamics in high-dimensional sensor and actuator data, facilitating effective decomposition of multivariate fault patterns. Adaptive Kalman filtering (AKF) and probabilistic signal smoothing enhance fault reconstruction while maintaining continuous control performance. The framework is supported by rigorous mathematical foundations, ensuring stability and convergence of the kernel-based algorithms. Leveraging kernel methods’ universal approximation capabilities, it achieves superior fault tolerance with real-time computational efficiency. Experimental validation shows 98.2 % fault detection accuracy across multiple sensor and actuator failure scenarios. Multi-scenario testing reveals significant improvements over uncompensated faults, including 90.5 % velocity error reduction, 91.7 % lateral error improvement, and 81.1 % angular error reduction. Compared to existing approaches focused on detection-only or requiring system interruption, this framework provides seamless real-time fault reconstruction. A comparative study against 14 state-of-the-art methods highlights its advantages in integrated control-diagnosis, nonlinear modeling, and continuous operation. This KPCA Digital Twin MPC framework establishes a new paradigm for fault-tolerant control in autonomous vehicles, bridging digital twin technology with practical, safety–critical applications.

title: Fault-tolerant control for micro-reactor sensors based on a PMSDC-LSTM-SE framework
abstract: This paper proposes a fault diagnosis and fault-tolerant control framework for sensor failures in micro-reactor systems. A sensor reconstruction model based on a Parallel Multi-Scale Dilated Convolutional Network (PMSDC), Long Short-Term Memory network (LSTM), and Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) channel attention mechanism is developed to reconstruct faulty sensor measurements from raw multivariate time-series signals. The reconstruction residual between the measured and estimated values is evaluated using Bayesian estimation to identify sensor faults and reduce false detection. The proposed selective Bayesian residual detection method achieves a false alarm rate of 0.00%, demonstrating improved reliability in distinguishing normal and faulty sensor states. After fault diagnosis, the faulty sensor is isolated and replaced with a redundant sensor to maintain control performance. Experimental results on a micro-reactor fault dataset demonstrate that the proposed method effectively identifies sensor fault types and severities, achieving average reductions of 53.5% in RMSE and 52.6% in MAE compared with the CNN-LSTM-based reconstruction approach. The proposed framework provides an effective solution for sensor fault diagnosis and fault-tolerant control in micro-reactor systems.

title: Layer-specific lipschitz modulation for fault-tolerant multimodal representation learning
abstract: Modern multimodal systems deployed in industrial and safety-critical environments must remain reliable under partial sensor failures, signal degradation, or cross-modal inconsistencies. This work introduces a mathematically grounded framework for fault-tolerant multimodal representation learning that unifies self-supervised anomaly detection and error correction within a single architecture. Building upon a theoretical analysis of perturbation propagation, we derive Lipschitz- and Jacobian-based criteria that determine whether a neural operator amplifies or attenuates localized faults. Guided by this theory, we propose a two-stage self-supervised training scheme: pre-training a multimodal convolutional autoencoder on clean data to preserve localized anomaly signals in the latent space, and expanding it with a learnable compute block composed of dense layers for correction and contrastive objectives for anomaly identification. Furthermore, we introduce layer-specific Lipschitz modulation and gradient clipping as principled mechanisms to control sensitivity across detection and correction modules. Experimental results on multimodal fault datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach improves both anomaly detection accuracy and reconstruction under sensor corruption. Overall, this framework bridges the gap between analytical robustness guarantees and practical fault-tolerant multimodal learning.
